rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. The resolution pattern will guide subsequent changes in gradient slope, starting composition, and temperature.

Keep the gradient fixed and test a substantial temperature change to reveal selectivity shifts within the central cluster and late doublet. The short initial elution window leaves room to slow the gradient afterward if necessary.

Reduce the gradient slope at the more promising temperature to spread the central cluster and test whether the near-coeluting pairs respond to slope. The current early elution suggests substantial room to improve resolution before incurring a time penalty.
The slower gradient resolves all but one pair without a time penalty. Lower temperature by one step to shift that pair's selectivity while checking that the resolved central peaks remain separated.

Use a shallower gradient to improve the remaining central pair, while raising the starting organic fraction to offset the longer elution time. This tests a route to full resolution with the last peak still near or below 10 minutes.

At 60 C the central cluster benefits from a slower gradient, but the 24-minute gradient creates a different near-coelution. Test an intermediate slope to seek a window where both groups are resolved, with ample margin below 10 minutes.

Increase the gradient slope by only 1.25% relative to injection 6, aiming to lift the 1.49-resolution pair above 1.5 while preserving the central separations. The gradient still extends beyond the observed elution window, so its lower endpoint should not compromise elution.

Injection 7 achieves the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark. Raise the starting organic fraction and narrow the gradient window to test a shorter fully resolved separation, with the slightly shallower slope helping preserve the central peak separations.

Slightly reduce the slope at the higher starting composition to recover the central pair that lost resolution in injection 8. This tests whether full resolution can be restored with a last-peak time shorter than the maximum-score benchmark.

Return to the successful starting composition and increase its gradient slope by just 1.85% relative to injection 7. This tests the faster edge of the fully resolved window while retaining injection 7 as the maximum-score fallback.

The faster boundary near injection 7 now appears constrained by central-pair resolution. Keep that maximum-score method as the benchmark and screen the low-temperature extreme for a different selectivity pattern that might support a faster fully resolved gradient.

Test a shallower gradient at 25 C to determine whether the two remaining critical pairs gain resolution. This explores the promising low-temperature selectivity pattern while retaining injection 7 as the maximum-score benchmark.

At 25 C, slowing the gradient worsened the central near-coelution, so test a faster gradient with a small temperature shift to adjust the late pair. Injection 7 remains the maximum-score benchmark while this explores a shorter separation.

Lower temperature while retaining the fast gradient to test whether the central separations improve relative to injection 13. Comparing directly with the 10-minute gradient at 25 C will also clarify the trade-off between central and late-pair resolution.

Test a higher starting composition with a shallower slope to alter the central cluster's selectivity while maintaining a short elution window. At 30 C the late pair already has useful resolution margin, making the central cluster the main target.

Test whether a further increase in starting organic fraction and lower temperature improve the remaining central pair while preserving the wider separations seen in injection 15. This explores a compact low-temperature separation without displacing the established maximum-score method.

Slightly slow the promising high-start gradient to improve the two pairs just below baseline resolution. Monitor the central pair currently at 1.72, since earlier low-temperature runs showed that excessive slowing can reduce its separation.

Injection 17 matches the maximum score with a much shorter separation. Raise the starting organic fraction and modestly reduce the slope to seek further time savings while protecting the marginal late pair.

Raise the starting organic fraction another step and use a shallower slope to protect the central pair as the elution window shifts earlier. Injection 18 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.

Return to the fully resolved starting composition from injection 18 and increase the slope by 10% to test its faster boundary. The central pair at R 1.61 is the limiting check; retain injection 18 if it falls below 1.5.

The faster slope crossed the central-pair resolution limit, so restore injection 18's gradient and test one temperature step higher. This checks whether temperature can shorten the separation without sacrificing full resolution.

Return to 25 C and reduce the slope at the higher starting composition to test whether the central pair can recover full resolution. This probes an alternative narrow-window method while retaining injection 18 as the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Refine around injection 18, the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method, with one step lower endpoint. This tests whether a modest time increase buys useful resolution margin, since both higher temperature and a steeper slope lost full resolution.

Test one further reduction in slope to improve resolution margin around the successful low-temperature method. Injection 18 remains the fastest fully resolved choice; this run targets a less marginal alternative while retaining the maximum CRF.

Preserve injection 18's successful slope while shortening the programmed gradient to four minutes. The gradient ends at the outlet at 4.65 minutes, after the expected last peak at 4.14 minutes, so this should retain full resolution and the maximum CRF.
